transcript.text: The back burner on our gas hob has gone a lazy yellow colour and leaves black soot on the pan. What's wrong with it?

A lazy yellow flame that leaves soot means the burner isn't getting enough air mixed with the gas, so it's burning incompletely. A healthy gas flame is crisp and mostly blue, perhaps with a small yellow tip. Incomplete combustion produces soot and can also produce carbon monoxide, so it's worth sorting out promptly.

## Common causes (roughly most to least likely)

1. Burner cap or crown not seated properly. If the cap has been knocked or put back slightly off-centre after cleaning, the flame pattern goes wrong. This is very common and easy to fix.
2. Blocked burner ports. Spilled food, grease or cleaning residue can clog the little holes around the burner head.
3. Wet burner. If it's been washed recently and isn't fully dry, it can burn badly until it dries out.
4. Partially blocked injector (jet). The small brass nozzle under the burner can get debris in it, which upsets the gas/air mix.
5. Air intake or mixing issue. Dust, grease or even a spider's web in the venturi tube (where air mixes with the gas) is a classic culprit.
6. Something more serious, such as a faulty injector, incorrect gas pressure, or the wrong jet fitted (e.g. after an LPG/natural gas conversion). These need a professional.

## Things you can safely check yourself

With the hob off and cool:

• Lift off the cap and burner head and check for food, grease or blockages.
• Clean the ports with a stiff brush or an unfolded paperclip/pin. Don't use a toothpick, as it can snap off inside.
• Wash and dry thoroughly (leave it a few hours or dry with a hairdryer).
• Reassemble carefully, making sure the cap sits flat and centred. It usually only fits one way, with a notch or lug that locates it.
• Light it and compare it with the other burners.

Don't try to adjust or remove the injector or anything beneath the burner unless you're qualified. In the UK, work on gas fittings must be done by a Gas Safe registered engineer.

## When to call an engineer

• The flame is still yellow and sooty after cleaning and reseating.
• More than one burner is affected.
• You notice a gas smell, the flame lifts off or roars, or anyone in the house has headaches, dizziness or nausea when the hob is on (possible CO symptoms).

## Safety in the meantime

• Avoid using that burner if possible, and keep the kitchen well ventilated.
• Make sure you have a working carbon monoxide alarm.
• If you ever smell gas, turn it off, open windows, don't use switches or flames, and call the National Gas Emergency number: 0800 111 999.

Most of the time this turns out to be a misaligned cap or clogged ports, so a good clean and careful reassembly is the best first step.

Thank you. You mentioned a gas smell, and now that I think of it, I have noticed a faint whiff of gas near the hob a few times in the mornings, even when all the knobs are off. Should I be doing something about that before I try cleaning the burner?

Yes. Deal with the gas smell first, and don't use or clean the hob until it's been checked. (My last message got cut off, but a gas smell was going to be top of the "call someone" list.)

A smell of gas with all the knobs off suggests a leak, possibly from a fitting, the hose or pipe behind the hob, or a tap inside the hob that isn't sealing fully. Noticing it in the mornings fits that pattern: a small leak can build up overnight when the kitchen is closed and still. Even if it's faint and intermittent, treat it as a gas escape.

## What to do now

1. Call the National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999 (free, 24/7). In Northern Ireland it's 0800 002 001. Tell them what you've told me: a faint, recurring smell near the hob with the controls off. They'll advise you and usually send someone out free of charge to find the leak and make it safe.
2. Open doors and windows to ventilate.
3. Don't create sparks or flames. Don't light the hob, smoke, or use matches or lighters. Avoid operating electrical switches (on or off), including light switches and plugs, near the area.
4. Turn off the gas at the meter if you can do so safely. The emergency control valve is a lever next to the meter. Turn it so it's at right angles to the pipe.
5. If the smell is strong at any point, get everyone out and make the call from outside.

## Afterwards

• The emergency service makes the supply safe but usually won't repair appliances. You'll then need a Gas Safe registered engineer to fix the leak and check the hob. Ask them to look at the yellow flame on the back burner too, since both problems may be related.
• If you don't already have one, fit a carbon monoxide alarm in the kitchen or nearby. A sooty yellow flame can produce CO, which has no smell, so the alarm covers a risk your nose can't.
• If anyone in the home has had headaches, dizziness, nausea or tiredness that improves away from the house, mention it to the engineer and see a doctor, as these can be signs of CO exposure.

Once an engineer has confirmed everything is safe, cleaning the burner as described earlier is fine to do.
